title: Mitochondria: Biochemistry and Clinical Significance
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Mitochondria generate ATP, regulate apoptosis, and are central to metabolic diseases. In low‑resource settings, defects present as lactic acidosis, myopathy, or cardiomyopathy. Recognise key tests and manage supportive care.

sections.p: Mitochondria are double‑membrane organelles that produce ATP via oxidative phosphorylation, regulate calcium, and initiate apoptosis. They contain their own DNA and ribosomes, allowing limited protein synthesis.
b: Inner membrane folds (cristae) increase surface area
Mitochondrial DNA encodes 13 proteins of the electron transport chain

sections.p: Glucose and fatty acids are oxidised to NADH and FADH₂, which donate electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC). Proton pumping creates a gradient that drives ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor.
b: Glycolysis → pyruvate → acetyl‑CoA → Krebs cycle → NADH/FADH₂
ATP synthase uses proton motive force

t.b: High lactate with normal oxygenation points to ETC defect
CK elevation signals muscle breakdown; very high levels (>10,000 U/L) raise suspicion of mitochondrial myopathy
Confirms pathogenic mutations; useful when clinical picture is unclear

sections.p: Mitochondrial biogenesis is driven by PGC‑1α, NRF1/2, and TFAM. Calcium uptake via the uniporter activates dehydrogenases, while ROS act as signalling molecules. Dysregulation leads to energy deficits.

Primary mitochondrial disorders arise from mtDNA or nuclear gene mutations. They manifest as lactic acidosis, exercise intolerance, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, or neurodegeneration. Secondary causes include infections (HIV, TB), toxins (antiretrovirals, isoniazid), and malnutrition.
b: Severe lactic acidosis can rapidly lead to shock and death if untreated

sections.p: Patients present with fatigue, muscle pain, exercise intolerance, or cardiomyopathy. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and basic labs. Management focuses on supportive care and avoiding mitochondrial toxins.
b: Consider referral for genetic counselling if family history

sections.p: Remember that lactic acidosis with normal oxygenation suggests mitochondrial disease. A high CK with normal creatinine points to myopathy. In resource‑poor settings, a bedside lactate meter and CK strip can guide management.
b: Avoid isoniazid in patients with unexplained fatigue or myalgia

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained sudden death in young patients

faq.q: How do I differentiate mitochondrial myopathy from muscular dystrophy?
faq.a: Mitochondrial myopathy shows exercise intolerance, ragged‑red fibres on biopsy, and elevated lactate; muscular dystrophy presents with progressive weakness and normal lactate.

faq.q: Can I use a bedside lactate meter in the ward?
faq.a: Yes, it is useful for detecting lactic acidosis; a reading >4 mmol/L warrants further investigation.

faq.q: What drugs should I avoid in suspected mitochondrial disease?
faq.a: Avoid drugs that inhibit the ETC such as valproate, isoniazid, linezolid, and high‑dose metformin.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with exercise intolerance and elevated CK presents with sudden cardiac arrest – what is the first step? — Check for arrhythmia, give anti‑arrhythmic, and consider implantable cardioverter.
A patient on isoniazid develops myalgia and elevated lactate – what is the most likely mechanism? — Inhibition of mitochondrial enzyme 2‑dehydropantoate 4‑phosphate?
A child with recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive has normal CBC but high lactate – what is the next investigation? — Serum lactate, CK, and consider mtDNA sequencing
A patient with HIV on zidovudine develops fatigue – what drug should be stopped? — Zidovudine (causes mitochondrial toxicity)
A 45‑year‑old man with chest pain and normal ECG but high CK‑MB – what does this suggest? — Myocardial injury due to mitochondrial dysfunction
A patient with TB on isoniazid develops severe lactic acidosis – what is the immediate management? — Stop isoniazid, give supportive care, monitor lactate
A 60‑year‑old with chronic heart failure and elevated lactate – what does this indicate? — Poor perfusion and possible mitochondrial dysfunction
A patient with suspected mitochondrial disease has normal creatinine but high CK – what does this imply? — Muscle breakdown, not renal failure
